subject: chem
title: Periodicity
subtitle: Trends across Period 3 and down Group 2 and Group 17.
concept: Physical and chemical properties show repeating (periodic) trends as atomic number increases, reflecting changes in electronic structure.
Across Period 3: atomic radius decreases, first IE increases (with dips at Mg→Al and P→S), electronegativity increases, metallic character decreases.
Melting points across Period 3 reflect bonding type: metals (Na–Al) then giant covalent (Si) then simple molecular (P₄, S₈, Cl₂, Ar).

notes.heading: Trends Across Period 3
items: Atomic radius decreases across Period 3: nuclear charge increases but all electrons are in the same shell (same shielding), so the effective nuclear charge increases and electrons are pulled closer to the nucleus.

First ionisation energy generally increases across the period. Two dips: Al < Mg (the 3p electron in Al is higher in energy and more shielded than the 3s electron in Mg) and S < P (the paired 3p electron in S experiences additional repulsion from its partner, making it easier to remove).

Electronegativity increases and metallic character decreases left to right. Melting points: Na–Al (metallic bonding, moderate) → Si (giant covalent, very high ≈ 1410 °C) → P₄, S₈, Cl₂ (simple molecular, low) → Ar (monatomic, very low).

notes.heading: Group 2 Trends
items: Reactivity increases down Group 2 as ionisation energy decreases (larger atoms, more shielded outer electrons). Mg reacts with steam; Ca reacts with cold water; Ba reacts vigorously.

Solubility of Group 2 sulfates decreases down the group — MgSO₄ is soluble, BaSO₄ is insoluble (used in barium meals because it is safe to ingest and opaque to X-rays). Solubility of hydroxides increases down the group — Ba(OH)₂ is the most soluble.
Thermal stability of carbonates increases down the group — a larger, more polarisable cation is less effective at distorting the carbonate ion, so more energy is needed for decomposition.

notes.heading: Group 17 Trends
items: Physical state at room temperature: F₂ (pale yellow gas), Cl₂ (yellow-green gas), Br₂ (orange-brown liquid), I₂ (grey-black solid). Volatility decreases (boiling point rises) because larger molecules have stronger id-id intermolecular forces.

Oxidising power (reactivity) decreases down the group: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂. A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide from solution. In cyclohexane extraction: Cl₂ → pale yellow, Br₂ → orange, I₂ → violet.

Reaction of sodium halides with concentrated H₂SO₄: NaCl → HCl (misty fumes, no redox); NaBr → HBr + SO₂ (Br⁻ reduces S from +6 to +4); NaI → HI + SO₂ + S + H₂S (I⁻ is a stronger reducing agent, reducing S all the way to −2).

definitions.body: The energy to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms.
The ability of an atom to attract the bonding electron pair in a covalent bond.
A more reactive halogen oxidises a halide ion of a less reactive halogen, displacing it from solution.

workedExamples.q: Explain why the first IE of sulfur is less than that of phosphorus.

steps.text: P: [Ne] 3s² 3p³ (half-filled 3p, one electron per orbital). S: [Ne] 3s² 3p⁴ (one 3p orbital has a paired electron).
The paired electron in S experiences extra electron-electron repulsion in the same orbital.
This repulsion makes the paired electron easier to remove, so IE of S < IE of P.

workedExamples.q: Cl₂ is bubbled into aqueous NaI. Describe and explain what is observed.

steps.text: Solution turns brown/orange (I₂ formed in solution); add cyclohexane: lower layer turns violet/purple (I₂ dissolves in non-polar solvent).
Cl₂ is a stronger oxidising agent than I₂; it oxidises I⁻ to I₂ and is itself reduced to Cl⁻.

mistakes: Confusing the dip in IE at Al (3p < 3s) with the dip at S (paired 3p electron).
Stating Group 2 hydroxide solubility decreases down group — it increases (Ba(OH)₂ is most soluble).
Forgetting to account for id-id forces when explaining trends in Group 17 boiling points.
tips: For halogen displacement: use cyclohexane (or hexane) to confirm identity — Cl₂ gives pale yellow, Br₂ gives orange, I₂ gives violet.
Solubility trends: 'Group 2 sulfates become less soluble; hydroxides become more soluble' down the group.
Always explain IE anomalies by reference to electron configuration.

flashcards.q: Why does atomic radius decrease across Period 3?
flashcards.a: Nuclear charge increases but electrons are in the same shell (same shielding), so electrons are pulled closer.

flashcards.q: Why is the first IE of Al lower than Mg?
flashcards.a: Al loses a 3p electron (higher energy than 3s), which is easier to remove than the 3s electron of Mg.

flashcards.q: What is observed when Cl₂ is added to KBr(aq)?
flashcards.a: Solution turns orange-brown — Br₂ is displaced; Cl₂ oxidises Br⁻ to Br₂.

flashcards.q: How does the oxidising power of halogens change down Group 17?
flashcards.a: Decreases — Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂ (electronegativity and electron affinity decrease).

flashcards.q: What type of structure does silicon have, and why is its MP so high?
flashcards.a: Giant covalent lattice; many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt it.

questions.q: Which element in Period 3 has the highest melting point?
questions.exp: Si has a giant covalent structure with many strong Si–Si bonds — very high MP (~1410°C).

questions.q: Why is the IE of S lower than that of P?
opts: S has a paired 3p electron that is easier to remove
questions.exp: The paired 3p electron in S experiences extra repulsion, making it easier to remove than P's half-filled 3p orbitals.

questions.q: Which Group 2 hydroxide is most soluble?
questions.exp: Solubility of Group 2 hydroxides increases down the group — Ba(OH)₂ is the most soluble.

questions.q: What colour does iodine give in cyclohexane?
questions.exp: I₂ dissolves in non-polar cyclohexane to give a characteristic violet/purple colour.

questions.q: Why does reactivity increase down Group 2?
opts: Ionisation energy decreases — easier to lose 2e⁻
questions.exp: Larger atoms: outer electrons are further from nucleus and more shielded → lower IE → easier to form M²⁺.

recall: Explain the trend in first IE across Period 3, including the two dips.
State and explain trends in Group 2: reactivity, solubility of sulfates and hydroxides.
Describe and explain halogen displacement reactions with test for each halogen.
Explain the variation in melting points across Period 3.
Explain why Group 17 boiling points increase down the group.
